client: I've been feeling so anxious about school lately. After failing that big exam last semester, I can't stop worrying that I'll lose my scholarship and disappoint everyone. I keep thinking "what if I fail again?" but the more I stress about it, the harder it is to focus when I try to study.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of worry about school. The fear of failing again seems to be creating a cycle where the anxiety itself makes it harder to focus. Would it help to explore some strategies to break this pattern?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess strategies could help, but I don't know if anything will work when the pressure feels so overwhelming. Every time I open my textbooks, my mind just goes blank and I start thinking about how much is riding on my grades. It's like my brain won't cooperate no matter how hard I try.
therapist: Your words capture how stuck you feel, but I notice your voice sounds more tense than your words suggest - like this really has you tied up in knots. When you say your brain won't cooperate, I wonder what that experience is like for you in those moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's like my thoughts start racing in circles - one minute I'm staring at the same paragraph for half an hour, the next I'm thinking about my parents' disappointed faces or how I'll have to drop out if I lose funding. My chest gets tight and I just end up pacing around my room instead of studying. I know it sounds dramatic, but it feels completely out of my control.
therapist: The way you describe this cycle - the racing thoughts leading to physical tension leading to avoidance - shows how very real this struggle is for you. You call it dramatic, but I hear you describing a truly distressing experience that makes perfect sense given the stakes. What happens if we try looking at this not as a character flaw, but as your mind's overprotective response to high pressure?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I never thought about it as my mind being overprotective - that's an interesting way to look at it. But even if it's trying to protect me, it's not helping. If anything, it's making things worse because I'm falling behind on my work. How do I get it to stop when the stakes feel so high?
therapist: I hear how frustrated you are with this pattern - it makes sense that you'd want it to stop when it's impacting your ability to stay on top of your work. While we can't turn off our protective instincts completely, we can try to gently redirect them. Would you be open to exploring some mindfulness techniques that could help create a bit more space between you and those anxious thoughts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I've tried some mindfulness apps before, but they just made me more frustrated because I couldn't quiet my mind like they said I should. It felt like one more thing I was failing at. But I'm willing to try again if there's a different approach - I just worry I'll get stuck in that same cycle of trying and failing.
therapist: It sounds like mindfulness has been frustrating in the past because it felt like another place you had to measure up to an ideal. Let's think differently about this - what if the goal wasn't to quiet your mind, but simply to notice when it starts racing without getting swept away in those thoughts? Would that feel more manageable to approach?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually does sound less intimidating than trying to force my thoughts to stop. But I'm not sure how to just "notice" them without getting caught up - when I'm in that panicked state, everything feels so urgent and real. What if I notice the thoughts but still can't pull myself out of them?
therapist: It's completely understandable that noticing your thoughts without getting caught up in them feels difficult right now - that sense of urgency and realness is part of what makes anxiety so powerful. How about we start small, with just a minute or two of noticing, and see how that goes? Remember, it's not about stopping the thoughts, but about creating a tiny bit of space from them.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Starting small with just a minute or two does sound less overwhelming. But I'm worried I'll get frustrated if I can't even do that much - sometimes my anxiety feels so intense that a minute feels like forever. What if I try and just end up feeling more discouraged?
therapist: Your concern about feeling discouraged is completely valid - anxiety can indeed make even short moments feel unbearable. Let's frame this as an experiment rather than a test, where whatever happens is useful information about what works (or doesn't work) for you. How does that approach feel?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Calling it an experiment does help take some pressure off. I think I could try that, as long as I remember that struggling with it doesn't mean I've failed. But I'm still nervous that when I'm in the middle of those anxious moments, I'll forget this perspective and just get overwhelmed again.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding two important truths - the willingness to try this new approach, alongside the very real concern that anxiety might still take over in those tough moments. That's actually a very balanced perspective to have. Would it help to brainstorm some gentle reminders you could use when you notice yourself getting overwhelmed?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, reminders might help... though I'm not sure what would actually get through to me in those moments. Everything seems so obvious when I'm calm like now, but when the anxiety hits, it's like I forget all the rational thoughts. Maybe something really simple, like "This is just anxiety" written on a sticky note? But will that really make a difference?
therapist: You're touching on something really important - how different things feel in anxious moments versus calmer times. A simple sticky note sounds like a great starting point, and what matters most is that this reminder feels useful to you, not whether it "should" work perfectly. Would you like to test it out and see what happens when the anxiety comes, then we can adjust based on your experience?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I'm willing to try the sticky notes, but I still have this nagging fear that I'll see it during an anxious moment and think "Yeah right, like this little note is going to help when my whole future is on the line." I guess I'm worried my anxiety will just dismiss any reminder, no matter how simple or kind.
therapist: I hear how your anxiety tries to convince you that small interventions couldn't possibly help with such big fears. That skeptical voice makes perfect sense - it's trying to protect you from disappointment. But what if we think of the sticky note not as a fix, but as a tiny interruption to that automatic anxious response, creating just enough space to try something different?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
